chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
title: Armstrong's March 1929 recording visit and the acoustic horns
summary: Armstrong's studio sessions the next days were difficult, with no microphones, no drums and the band scattered around horns.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: And on that two-day visit that Armstrong made to New York, that's when you went in the recording studio.
We went in the recording studio the next day.
And that actually, according to Rust, was on March 5, 1929.
Yeah. And we started making a series of records and things. I don't know, I think we was makin'...I think was makin' "I Can't Give You Anything But Love."
Yes, that's correct. You recorded that.

I know it had taken us the whole session to make one side -- "I Can't Give You Anything But Love." We came back to the studio again, I think it was the day he finished, the next day after he finished at the Savoy. He was only there two nights. And the day after, when he finished at the Savoy, we was back in the studio again makin' some more records.
In fact, Louis kept us pretty busy there the short time that he was in New York.
Now, why it took so long to do "I Can't Give You Anything But Love" was because they really were trying to feature Louis, or...?
Oh, it was Louis. Everything was Louis.

Everything had to be perfect for him, according to the technicians. They were the ones back in the room with the stuff on their ears, and this-that-and-the-other, placing him here and placing the horns there. In them days, you didn't have no microphones up there. It was strictly a thing with a whole lot of horns, and you'd play into the horns.

Recording was very hard in them days. It was very tough. Because you weren't allowed to use drums, so you had no drums. You had a brass section, and the brass would way back in the back someplace. The reeds would be up in the front by the horns, and the brass would be someplace. and Louis might be blowing out the window somewhere! You know what I mean? Everything was disruptive. Not like the recording is today. A band goes in today, and they play just like they're on the bandstand, at ease; I mean, they play the same way. But not in them days. You just barely whispered into your horn. You could just barely hear it, you know. I don't know how they got such good recordings as they did, because they got some wonderful recordings, under the systems that they were using. But it was tough, it was tough.
